dehydrated_text:
It's all false; it's all what we imagine it to be. One day, for whatever reason, one of us, the chains disappear, and we stumble upwards out of the cave. Now we're suddenly in the light, right? We see the sun, which is Asha truth, or a haram master. We're blinded because our eyes are used to seeing the dark; we can't see at first. But over time, we start to see more clearly and realize the world is beautiful. We see the birds flying in the sky, the trees around us, and the animals. We feel, "This is beautiful." I found heaven.

I found the truth. I found Asha. I have found a haram master. This is what life is really about. But after some time, you realize this isn't enough. I have found the truth, but the truth is not complete because I know there are my friends and family that are stuck inside the cave. Therefore, to fully achieve Asha, I must go down and tell them the truth. Tell them there is an Asha, and we can all break through our chains, escape into the light, and see the truth for ourselves, then be truly happy and free and wise.

Asha is not just breaking through your chains and seeing the truth for yourself; it's a responsibility to go and spread this virtue to everyone around you. If you see injustice, speak out. A metaphor can help: a choir singing in harmony. Our master, the monad, sings a song, and we have to sing along with him. When we do that, the world is harmonized, perfect, beautiful. But if most of us are out of tune, we need to get into tune.

So, Asha is helping others see the truth for themselves. If you yourself see the truth, you now have a responsibility to teach this truth to others. The problem is, when you go down and tell everyone, "Hey man, this world we're living in is a shadow world. It's a prison. We need to break our chains and escape into the real world," they'll likely say, "You're crazy." Get out of here, man. You're crazy. But if you persist, they might ask, "Okay, well then describe this world to us." And you'll find it hard to explain.

That's Plato's allegory of the cave. This gives a better understanding of the idea of Asha. If you move towards the truth, you're moving towards Asha. But if you're moving away from Asha, you're moving towards Drew. That's a basic premise of Zorashinism. This is the idea that Zorus brought to the world and will forever change it.

We don't know when Zorathusa lived; estimates place him between 2000 B.C.E. and around 1500 BC, during the Bronze Age. During this time, people were in love with capitalism, wanting to get rich. But as the system matured, there was slavery, debt, corruption, misery, suffering—people wanted another voice. Zorathusa himself was a priest who was disgusted by the corruption among priests because being a priest meant leading people into the light and Asha. However, once the branches became more mature, priests were corrupt, wanting money for helping achieve immortality and spreading false teachings. Disgusted, Zorathusa wandered around spreading his new message of Asha.
